segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that for -ar verbs, we take away the -ar and we put -aba to get this line in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So cenar, to dine or to have dinner; cenaba, I was having dinner, I was dining, I used to have dinner, I used to dine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now for -er/-ir verbs, we take away our -er/-ir ending and we put -ía. Where did we hear that before? -ía.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: The "would" tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comer was to eat. How was I would eat?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comería.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comería, good. Now, for the line in the past, we're not adding on to the full verb, we're taking off our ending before we put -ía. So how would it be I was eating, he was eating, she was eating, etc.?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comía. Vender is to sell, vender. I would sell it. I would sell it.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo vendería.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo vendería. I was selling it? I was selling it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo vendía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo vendía, good. If you want to say for sale, you can just say it sells itself. It sells itself, it's for sale. How would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se vende.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se vende, good, for sale, se vende, it sells itself. And if you go to a Spanish-speaking place, you will see on houses and on cars this expression: se vende. It was selling itself? It was for sale?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se vendía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se vendía. It would be for sale? It would sell itself?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se vendería.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se vendería. It would sell itself, it would be for sale, good. What was to break again, related to rupture?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Romper.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Romper, good. How would you say I was breaking it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo rompía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo rompía, good. And if you just want to say it was breaking, and you mean by itself, it was breaking not something else, how would you say it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se rompía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se rompía, good. How would you say they were breaking?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se rompían.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se rompían, good. Give me again the "to" form, to break?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Romper.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Romper. What is I would break it? I would break it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo rompía. Ah. Lo rompería.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo rompería. I would break it. How would you say I was breaking it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo rompía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo rompía, good. How would you say they would break it? They would break it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Les...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: They would break is where you need to begin.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Romperían. Lo romperían.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo romperían. They were breaking it? They were breaking it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo rompían.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo rompían. So, we have the same endings for "would" and for the line in the past for -er/-ir verbs. The big difference of course is that for "would" we are adding on to the "to" form of the verb, and for the past, we're taking off our endings first, which means we get pairs like comería, I would eat; comía, I was eating. Rompería, I would break; rompía, I was breaking.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say it breaks? It breaks, and you mean it gets broken, it breaks itself, in the present tense?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se rompe.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se rompe. How would you say it's going to break? It's going to break?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How is we are going, or let's go?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, vamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It is going to break?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se va a romper.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Se va a romper or va a romperse. So this means it's going to break. It's going to get broken. And there we're not waiting to hear what it's going to break because we have se. So we've completed that structure, we've completed the sentence with se.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for how in Spanish is cómo. If you want to ask somebody in Spanish how do you say, so maybe you have a Spanish-speaking friend that speaks English and you want to use them like a dictionary and say how do you say XYZ, what you will say in Spanish is how does it say itself? How is it said? How does it say itself?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is another example of where you might be using this structure of self, which we are seeing in Spanish is very flexible. It's giving us many different meanings, this structure of myself, yourself, ourselves, itself, this structure. So it says from decir is dice.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's a little bit irregular, but then the other versions follow. So we have dice for he, she, it, usted. How would you say you informal say?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dices.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, and they?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dicen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dicen. And as we know, the we form tends to escape the irregularity as the accent is somewhere else, so we go back to decir, and to say we say?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Decimos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Decimos, good. So how would you say how is it said, how does it say itself?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Cómo se dice?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Cómo se dice? So you you will use this often. You don't say cómo dices. This means how do you as an individual say, how do you say it? If you want to say how is it said, ¿cómo se dice? How does it say itself?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So se is doing quite a lot in Spanish. Sometimes we're using it to wrap up the sentence to show that we're not using a verb to anybody or to anything else, like in it breaks or it transforms, these examples that we saw. Sometimes the se is changing the meaning like between quedar, remain or be left over, and quedarse, to stay. And sometimes this se has quite a creative application: se vende, it sells itself, for sale. Or we could even have se habla, se habla español, Spanish speaks itself, Spanish is spoken, Spanish spoken, se habla español.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quedar by itself means to remain, and you can use this in the sense of I have one left. In Spanish, you will say it remains to me one. This is the structure in Spanish: I have one left, it remains to me one. So how would you say that: I have one left? What is the word for one?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Uno.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Uno, or una if you're talking about a feminine thing. So, I have one left, it remains to me one?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me quedo uno.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That means I stay one. So there, you made the reflexive structure, you said I remain myself and you got the meaning of to stay. But what you want is it remains to me.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me queda uno.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me queda uno. I have one left. Me queda uno. I have two left. If me queda uno is it remains to me one, I have one left, how do you think you would say I have two left? The word for two is dos, dos.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Related to dual. So, I have two left, they remain to me two?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me quedan dos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me quedan dos, very good. And of course we have the they form of the verb because it's they remain. As I'm saying they remain to me, to me, how do you think it would be if you wanted to say he has two left?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Le quedan dos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Le quedan dos. Two of them, they remain to him: le quedan dos. He has two left, or she has two left, or you formal have two left.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So maybe if you go to a shop and you ask for something and there's none left, maybe they will say no me quedan, I don't have any left. No me quedan, no me queda, you will hear both, just depending on what the person has in their mind. I have none left as in one, I have none left as in they've all gone. No me queda, no me quedan.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But we saw that with this verb then when we use this reflexive structure, this self structure, we get a different meaning. If I say I remain myself, then I get the meaning of to stay, I stay. So how is I remain myself?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me quedo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me quedo. We remain ourselves?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nos quedamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nos quedamos, good. He remains himself, or she remains herself?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se queda.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se queda. They stay?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se quedan.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se quedan, good. It's all of those that begin with L: él, lo, la, los, las all become se for the self version. From hablar, to speak, if you want to say I was speaking, he was speaking?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaba. So we have -aba as our key sound for the line in the past for -ar verbs. They were speaking?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaban.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say they were staying, they were remaining themselves?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se quedaban.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se quedaban, good. They weren't staying here?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No se quedaban aquí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I wasn't staying here?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No me quedaba... no.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So -aba works for I, he, she, it, the you formal.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No me quedaba... No me quedaba aquí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No me quedaba aquí. And we were staying here?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nos quedábamos aquí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The accent stays.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quedábamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nos quedábamos aquí. We weren't staying here?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No nos quedábamos aquí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No nos quedábamos aquí, good. Now, if you wanted to say we didn't have any left, so here what we will say is it didn't, or they didn't, we have the option, remain to us.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No nos quedaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No nos quedaba or no nos quedaban. Good.
